name: Rosa Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a dozer operator at the Redlands bauxite mine, the red dirt you make aluminium from. Half my week I'm pushing up stockpiles and clearing ahead of the excavators, and the other half I'm on rehab, which is putting the land back after we've mined it: spreading the topsoil, shaping the slopes so the seedlings take. I love the rehab work, honestly, you drive past a patch you did six years ago and there are birds nesting in it. The early starts are what wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does AI fit into your life right now, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, a bit. I use an assistant on my phone to plan meals, to read the long safety documents and tell me what's changed, and to help with my drone. I bought a cheap drone two years ago and I make little videos of the rehab sites, the environmental team loves them. My husband Gianni drove buses until he retired, and his pension is small. We redid the roof and paid off the car this year, so there's barely three weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a bit of a letdown, I was having fun with it. At work I'd say it's still handy for the paperwork. I'd probably post a drone video with some joke about the robots not coming after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's fine for me. My plan was always to work to about sixty-three and do a bit of drone work on the side. Nothing in this picture changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. I'd keep using the assistant and maybe pay for the proper drone licence this year, about six hundred. And I'd put a little away each fortnight to build us back up after the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the environmental team loves your videos. Has that ever turned into anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They asked me to fly the old pits for their yearly report last spring, off the clock, just as a favour. I said yes because I wanted to see it from up there. I've moved half a hillside with a dozer, and it took a drone to show me what it looked like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job that's already changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dozers have GPS guidance now, the blade sort of knows where to go. Some of the older men hate it. I love it, it means I can concentrate on the bits that need a person.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown because I was having fun with AI, but it's still handy for paperwork. I'd post a drone video with a joke about the robots not coming after all.
S0.think: Privately it's fine for me, because my plan was always to work to about sixty-three with some drone work on the side. Nothing here changes that.
S0.do: Keeps working and using her AI assistant daily. Pays about six hundred for a proper drone licence and puts a little away each fortnight to rebuild savings after the roof repair.
S0.quote: I've moved half a hillside with a dozer, and it took a drone to show me what it looked like.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa is curious and cheerful about technology, from her dozer's GPS guidance to the drone she flies for the environmental team. She is pragmatic rather than political and her plans are small and concrete. Her thin savings come from one-off costs rather than poor habits, which shapes how relaxed she sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift but there'll be work for people who learn the new stuff. The company should help people retrain, not just leave them to it. I'd be the one at the break table showing people the apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be all right. The stockpile pushing might go to self-driving dozers, but rehab needs judgement, and someone has to fly the drones and check the machines. I'd be quite happy to swap the cab for a laptop and a drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the environmental manager in the first month and ask if they'd take me on for surveying and rehab monitoring, even part-time. I'd get the drone licence straight away, not next year. And I'd start charging small farms nearby for drone photos of their fences and dams, fifty or a hundred a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually, and a bit excited. It's the first time in years work's felt like it could go somewhere new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're calm, but your savings are thin. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does a bit, I won't pretend. But a thin cushion's a reason to move early, not to sit still. If I wait to see what happens, I'm the one they don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Kev, he's sixty-one and won't even use the GPS. Kev says the machine doesn't know where the soft ground is, and he's right, but the machine doesn't need a tea break either.

S1.say: I'd say it's a big shift but there'll be work for people who learn the new tools, and the company should help them retrain. I'd be the one at the break table showing people the apps.
S1.think: Off the record, I think I'd be all right, because rehab needs judgement and someone has to fly the drones and check the machines. I'd be happy to swap the cab for a laptop and a drone.
S1.do: Asks the environmental manager in the first month for surveying and rehab monitoring work and gets her drone licence straight away. Starts charging nearby farms fifty to a hundred a job for drone photos of fences and dams.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, as if work could go somewhere new.
S1.quote: Kev says the machine doesn't know where the soft ground is, and he's right, but the machine doesn't need a tea break either.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa treats thin savings as a reason to move early, not to wait, which is the key to her calm. She has a concrete route into rehab monitoring and a small drone side business. Her affection for her colleague Kev, who refuses even GPS, shows she can see who gets left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough and people need help fast, from the government and the companies. I'd try to be practical about it, share what's working, not just doom. But I'd admit it's scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years is too quick for my drone plan to matter. If AI can do almost any work, it can fly the drone and read the rehab data too. I'd be sixty with three weeks in the bank and a retired husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go to the environmental team first, because the first year someone has to set up the new systems and I know the ground. I'd push the side work hard, every farm, every wedding, anything, and bank every dollar. And I'd ask Gianni's bus depot if they're short of anything, since people still need driving for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, clearly. But I can still see moves to make, so not panicked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what does two years buy you, compared with no warning at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one good year of being useful while they change over. Two years is enough to be the person who shows the robot the site, and then that's the end of the tour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Gianni. What would you say to him that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we've been poor before and we'll be poor again, we're good at it. He'd laugh. Then we'd both sit up doing the numbers on my phone.

S2.say: I'd say it's going to be rough and people need fast help from the government and companies. I'd try to share what works rather than just doom, but I'd admit it's scary.
S2.think: Privately, two years is too quick for my drone plans to matter, because AI could fly the drone and read the rehab data too. I'd be sixty with three weeks of savings and a retired husband.
S2.do: Goes to the environmental team to help set up the new systems during the changeover year. Pushes drone side work hard, banks every dollar, and asks her husband's old bus depot about short-term work.
S2.feel: Clearly anxious, but she can still see moves to make.
S2.quote: Two years is enough to be the person who shows the robot the site, and then that's the end of the tour.
S2.fieldNote: Two years is the first picture that worries Rosa properly, because it removes the human role she was moving into. She still finds moves, which keeps her short of alarm. The line about showing the robot the site captures her clear view of being useful only for a short window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to move if people start now, and I'd tell everyone to start now. Learn the tools, get a licence, get a side thing. I'd probably make a little video about it for the town's online group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three, which is my plan. I'd use those years in the rehab and drone work and step off just as things fully switch. It's tight, but it fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, drone licence, rehab monitoring role, and a proper little business for the farms. I'd aim for a few hundred a month extra and put it all aside. I'd also teach the older operators the GPS and the apps, because the company would pay someone to do that and it might as well be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's like a long drive with a deadline, you just keep your foot down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years versus two. What's the real difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years I'm scrambling for one year of use. Five years, I'm the bridge, I get to be the person who gets everyone else across. That's a job I'd actually like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about what happens to the land itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Rehab done by robots might be done to the letter and still look wrong. I'd want someone checking it with their eyes, and I'd say so in every meeting.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to move if people start now: learn the tools, get a licence, get a side income. I'd make a video about it for the town's online group.
S3.think: Off the record, five years puts me at sixty-three, which is my plan. I'd spend the years in rehab and drone work and step off as the switch finishes.
S3.do: Gets the drone licence and a rehab monitoring role in the first year and builds a small farm drone business worth a few hundred a month, all saved. Offers to teach older operators GPS and apps as a paid role.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, like a long drive with a deadline.
S3.quote: Five years, I'm the bridge, I get to be the person who gets everyone else across.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Rosa's own retirement timing, and she sees herself as a bridge helping others across. Her worry shifts partly to the land, and whether robot rehab would look right. She is practical and cheerful but honest about being on a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time if you use it. The young ones should be learning now. I'd be telling everyone to get going, but nicely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be retired by then, sixty-eight, flying my drone over the dam for fun. So for me this is the best of the three AGI ones. I'd just worry for the grandkids and the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before but less rush: licence, rehab work, side business, save a bit each fortnight. I'd also help our daughter's boy pick a trade, maybe something like robot servicing or the solar farms. And I'd keep teaching the older crews the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost cheerful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that bothers you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will waste it. Ten years sounds like forever until it's gone. My Gianni drove the same bus route for thirty years and never once thought about the bus driving itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to fix things and learn to talk to people, those two together. The robot can do one or the other for a while. And don't follow your grandmother into the mine.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is loads of time if you use it, and the young ones should be learning now. I'd tell everyone to get going, but nicely.
S4.think: Privately, I'd be sixty-eight and retired by then, flying my drone for fun, so this is the best of the AGI pictures for me. I'd just worry for my grandchildren and the town.
S4.do: Follows the same plan at a gentler pace: drone licence, rehab work, a side business and regular savings. Helps her grandson choose a trade such as robot servicing or solar, and keeps teaching older crews the new tools.
S4.quote: My Gianni drove the same bus route for thirty years and never once thought about the bus driving itself.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Rosa's own retirement is safely ahead of the change, and her mood is the lightest of all. Her concern is that people waste long warnings, illustrated by her husband's thirty years on one bus route. Her advice to her grandson pairs practical skills with people skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to be the bridge, you just fall in the river with everyone else. What would help is the company paying for retraining early, before they need to, and some money for older workers to get to their pensions. I don't mind changing, I've changed my whole life, I just need someone to give me the runway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the land. Everyone talks about jobs, but we dig the country up and promise to put it back. I'd want to know a person still checks that it's done right.

headlineQuote: I don't mind changing, I've changed my whole life, I just need someone to give me the runway.
portrait: Rosa Rossi is 58 and drives a dozer at the Redlands bauxite mine, splitting her time between pushing stockpiles and rehab work, putting mined land back. She uses an AI assistant every day, flies a drone for the environmental team and has under a month of savings after a roof repair, with her husband Gianni retired on a small bus driver's pension. She treats thin savings as a reason to move early, so she stays calm under hype and steady disruption, aiming for drone surveying and rehab monitoring. AGI in two years makes her anxious because it removes the human role she was moving into, while five and ten years fit her plan to stop at sixty-three. She cares about the people left behind and about whether the land is put back properly.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there's no time to move into a new role before it disappears too.
whatWouldHelp: The company paying for retraining early, and money to help older workers reach their pensions.
